title: am / is / are
pattern: subject + am / is / are + adjective / place
meaning: the verb “be”: every sentence that describes something or a place needs it
why: Every English sentence needs a verb. To describe someone, say how they are, or say where they are, use am / is / are.
form: I am · he / she / it is · you / we / they are
Negative: isn't / aren't · Question: Is she…? Are you…?
us: Americans almost always use the short forms: I'm, he's, it's, we're, they're. The full “I am” is for emphasis: I am ready!
mistakes: An English sentence always needs a verb.
examples: I'm really tired today.
She's at work right now.
We're not ready yet.
Is your brother married?

quiz.why: “she” → is, and in a question it comes first
You need a verb, and “food” is singular → is

title: Present simple (-s with he / she / it)
meaning: present simple: a habit or a fact, with -s after he / she / it
why: For things that happen always or usually, and for facts. With he / she / it, the verb gets -s. Forgetting it is the most common mistake.
form: I / you / we / they work · he / she / it works
go → goes · watch → watches · study → studies · have → has
us: Americans say it fast and the -s is sometimes hard to hear, but you still have to say it and write it.
examples: My dad works from home.
She usually takes the bus.
It rains a lot here in winter.
He always has coffee in the morning.

quiz.q: My brother ___ to the gym every day.

title: do / does / did: questions and negatives
pattern: Do / Does / Did + subject + base verb…?
meaning: questions and negatives: do / does / did + the base verb
why: In the present and past simple, you can't make a question or a negative with the main verb alone. Add do, does, or did, and the verb goes back to its base form (no -s, no -ed).
form: Do you…? · Does he…? · Did they…?
I don't · she doesn't · we didn't + base verb
us: In speech, don't, doesn't, and didn't are always short. “Did you…?” often sounds like “Didja…?”.
examples: Do you want some tea?
Does she know about it?
I didn't see him yesterday.
He doesn't eat meat.

title: Present continuous: now and plans
meaning: something happening now, or an arranged plan
why: am / is / are + verb-ing: for something happening right now or around now. Also for plans that are already arranged (tomorrow, this week).
form: I'm working · she's working · they're working
A plan: I'm meeting him tomorrow.
us: Americans use it a lot for plans: “What are you doing tonight?”
mistakes: You need am / is / are before -ing.
know, like, and want usually don't take -ing.
examples: I'm cooking dinner right now.
She's staying with her cousin this week.
What are you doing tonight?
We're flying to Dubai on Friday.

title: Past simple
meaning: something that happened and finished in the past
why: For something that happened and finished at a known time (yesterday, last year). Regular verbs take -ed; irregular verbs must be learned (go → went).
form: work → worked · go → went · see → saw · have → had
Questions and negatives with did: Did you go? · I didn't go.
us: In American English, the past simple is used even with just, already, and yet: “Did you eat yet?” “I just got here.”
examples: We went to the beach last weekend.
I called you twice this morning.
Did you finish your homework?
She didn't say anything.

quiz.q: I ___ a great movie last night.

quiz.why: A question in the past → did

title: a / an / the
pattern: a / an + one thing · the + the known thing
meaning: a / an for something new or any one; the for the known one
why: a / an: one thing you mention for the first time, or any one (a car). the: a thing we both know or already mentioned (the car). For things in general, no article (I love music).
form: a + consonant sound: a book, a university
an + vowel sound: an apple, an hour
the = the known one · no article = in general
us: Americans say “go to the hospital” and “in the hospital” (British English: in hospital).
examples: I need a new phone.
The phone you gave me is great.
He's an engineer.
I love music, but I hate the noise here.

quiz.why: “hour” starts with a vowel sound (the h is silent)

title: there is / there are
meaning: there is / there are: something exists or doesn't
why: To say something exists (or doesn't). there is for one thing, there are for more than one; negative: there isn't / there aren't.
form: There's a… · There are some… · Is there…? · Are there any…?
us: In casual speech people even say “There's a lot of people”, but “There are” is more correct.
mistakes: To say something exists, use “there is”, not “have”.
examples: There's a pharmacy near my house.
There are a lot of people here.
Is there a bathroom here?
There isn't any milk left.

quiz.q: Which one means “it's not a problem”?

title: Question word order
meaning: in a question, the helping verb comes before the subject
why: In a question, the helping verb comes before the subject: Where do you live? — not Where you live? This is a common mistake when your first language doesn't change word order for questions.
form: Wh- + do / does / did / is / can… + subject + verb
What do you do? · Where is she? · Why did he leave?
us: In fast speech: “Whaddya want?” = What do you want? “Where'd you go?” = Where did you go?
examples: Where do you work?
What time does the store open?
Why did you leave so early?
How long have you been here?

title: much / many / a lot of / some / any
pattern: many + countable · much + uncountable · a lot of + both
meaning: a lot / how many / how much: it depends on whether you can count it
why: many for things you can count (cars), much for things you can't (money, time). a lot of works for both. some in positive sentences, any in questions and negatives.
form: How many friends? · How much money?
a lot of + anything · some / any
us: Americans rarely use “much” in positive sentences; they say “a lot of time”, not “much time”. “lots of” is casual and natural.
examples: How many kids do they have?
I don't have much time today.
She has a lot of friends.
Do we have any bread?

quiz.q: We had ___ fun at the party.

title: I / me / my / mine
meaning: the pronoun changes with its job: subject, object, or owner
why: I is the subject (I do it), me is the object (he calls me), my goes before a noun (my book), mine stands alone (it's mine). The same with he / him / his, she / her / hers, they / them / their.
form: I – me – my – mine · he – him – his · she – her – her(s)
we – us – our – ours · they – them – their – theirs
us: “Me and him went” is common in casual American speech, but “He and I went” is correct. “Who did you see?” is more common than “whom”.
mistakes: After a preposition or a verb → me.
examples: Can you help me with this?
That's not my bag. Mine is black.
I saw her at the mall.
Is this car theirs?

quiz.q: Is this your phone? No, ___ is in my pocket.
I called ___ yesterday, but she didn't answer.

title: will vs going to (gonna)
pattern: be going to + verb · will + verb
meaning: the future: a plan (going to) or a decision or promise (will)
why: going to: a plan you already made, or something you can see is about to happen. will: a decision you make now, a promise, or a general prediction.
form: I'm going to + verb (a plan) · I'll + verb (a decision now / a promise)
us: In speech, “going to” sounds like “gonna”: I'm gonna call him. Use it when speaking, not in formal writing.
examples: I'm going to start a new job next month.
I'll call you when I get home.
Don't worry, I'll help you.
Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.

quiz.q: The phone is ringing. I ___ get it.
We ___ visit my aunt this weekend. We planned it.

title: can / could: ability and requests
pattern: Can I get…? · Could you + verb…?
meaning: can / could: ability and polite requests
why: can for ability, permission, and requests. could for ability in the past, and for more polite requests.
form: can / can't + verb · could / couldn't + verb
A request: Can I…? Could you…?
us: In American restaurants and stores, people say “Can I get a…?” to order. “can't” is pronounced clearly: /kænt/.
examples: Can I get a large coffee, please?
Could you open the window?
I couldn't sleep last night.
She can speak three languages.

quiz.q: When I was young, I ___ run fast.

title: in / on / at for time
pattern: at + time · on + day · in + month / year
meaning: at for a time, on for a day, in for a month or a year
why: at for a clock time or a moment (at 5:00, at night), on for a day or a date (on Monday), in for a month, a year, or a part of the day (in July, in the morning).
form: at 7 · at night · at noon
on Friday · on May 3rd
in 2024 · in summer · in the evening
us: American English: “on the weekend” (British: at the weekend). “on Monday” is sometimes dropped: “See you Monday!”
examples: The meeting is at ten.
What are you doing on the weekend?
I was born in 1998.
I usually study in the evening.

title: Comparatives and superlatives
meaning: bigger than / the biggest
why: Short adjectives take -er and the -est (big → bigger → the biggest). Long ones take more and the most. Use than to compare.
form: cheap → cheaper → the cheapest
expensive → more expensive → the most expensive
good → better → the best · bad → worse → the worst
us: In speech, “He's taller than me” is much more common than “than I am”. “way better” = much better.
examples: This phone is cheaper than that one.
It's the best restaurant in town.
Today is way hotter than yesterday.
Her new apartment is more comfortable.

quiz.q: That was the ___ day of my life.

title: Present perfect: have done
meaning: a life experience, or something from the past until now
why: It links the past to now: an experience in your life (Have you ever…?), something that happened and still matters now, or something that started in the past and is still going on. It doesn't go with a finished time like “yesterday”.
form: have / has + V3: I've seen · she's been · they've finished
Have you ever…? · I've never… · not … yet
us: Americans use it less than the British: with just, already, and yet they often use the past simple: “Did you eat yet?” “I already did it.” Both are correct in American English.
mistakes: From a time until now → present perfect.
examples: Have you ever been to Turkey?
I've never tried sushi.
She's lost her keys again.
We've known each other for years.

title: for / since / How long…?
meaning: for a length of time, since a starting point
why: for with a length of time (for two years), since with the starting point (since 2019, since Monday). The question: How long have you…?
form: for + a length of time: for ten minutes, for a long time
since + a starting point: since last year, since I was a kid
us: In speech: “It's been ages!” = it's been a long time. “I've been here for like an hour” (like = about).
examples: I've been waiting for twenty minutes.
She's worked here since 2021.
How long have you had this car?
It's been ages since we last talked.

quiz.q: I've lived in Erbil ___ five years.

title: Past continuous: was doing
pattern: was / were + verb-ing … when + past simple
meaning: something was happening, and something else interrupted it
why: was / were + -ing: something that was in progress at a moment in the past, often interrupted by something else in the past simple (when).
form: I / he / she was + -ing · you / we / they were + -ing
I was cooking when he called.
us: Americans often start stories this way: “So I was walking down the street, and…”
examples: I was taking a shower when you called.
What were you doing at nine last night?
It was raining all day.
We were watching TV when the power went out.

quiz.why: It was in progress and got interrupted

quiz.q: While I was driving, my phone ___.
quiz.why: The thing that interrupted → past simple

title: used to + verb
meaning: a habit in the past that is over now
why: A past habit that isn't true anymore: I used to smoke (I don't now). Questions and negatives: Did you use to…? / didn't use to.
form: used to + base verb
Did you use to…? · I didn't use to…
us: It sounds like “yoost-ta”. would is also used for old habits in stories: “My grandma would make bread every Friday.”
mistakes: In a positive sentence, “used” has a d.
“be used to” means “be accustomed to” — something different.
examples: I used to live in Guadalajara.
We used to play soccer every Friday.
Did you use to have long hair?
She didn't use to like coffee.

options: I smoked before, and I stopped.
quiz.why: An old habit that is over

title: First conditional: if + present, will
meaning: if something (possible) happens, something else will happen
why: For something that may really happen in the future: if + present simple, and will in the result. Don't put will after if.
form: If + present simple, … will + verb
If it rains, we'll stay home.
us: In speech, the result often comes first: “I'll call you if I'm late.” unless = if not.
mistakes: “will” goes in the result, not after “if”.
examples: If you're hungry, I'll make you something.
If it rains tomorrow, we'll cancel the trip.
I'll text you if I'm going to be late.
Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.

quiz.q: If you ___ early, we'll go together.
If she calls, I ___ tell her.

options: If I will see him, I'll tell him.
If I see him, I'll tell him.
If I see him, I tell him tomorrow.

title: Second conditional: if + past, would
meaning: if (imagined), something would happen
why: For something imaginary or unlikely now: if + past simple, and would in the result. If I had money, I'd travel.
form: If + past simple, … would + verb
If I were you, I'd…
us: The formal form is “If I were you”; in casual American speech “If I was you” is very common. “I'd” = I would.
examples: If I had more time, I'd learn to play the guitar.
If I were you, I'd ask for more time.
What would you do if you won the lottery?
She'd be happier if she lived closer to her family.

quiz.q: If I ___ rich, I'd buy a big house.
If you had a car, you ___ drive to work.
“If I were you” is used to:
quiz.why: give advice (in your place, I would…)

title: have to / must / should / don't have to
pattern: have to + verb · should + verb · don't have to + verb
meaning: it's necessary, it's a good idea, it isn't necessary
why: have to = it's necessary (a rule or a situation). must = it's necessary (your own opinion, or written rules). should = it's a good idea (advice). don't have to = it isn't necessary, but mustn't = it's not allowed.
form: I have to work · she has to · I had to
you should… · you don't have to… · you mustn't…
us: Americans rarely use “must” for obligation; they say “I have to” or “I've got to” = “I gotta go”. “must” is common for guessing: “You must be tired.”
examples: I have to get up early tomorrow.
You should see a doctor.
You don't have to pay now.
I've got to go, see you later.

quiz.why: gotta = have got to = I have to

title: -ing or to + verb
meaning: some verbs take -ing and some take to
why: Some verbs are followed by -ing (enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, keep) and some by to (want, need, decide, hope, plan). After a preposition, always -ing.
form: enjoy / finish / mind / keep + -ing
want / need / decide / plan + to + verb
stop doing = quit · stop to do = stop in order to do it
us: “I'm thinking about moving” and “Do you mind waiting?” are very common in American speech.
examples: I enjoy cooking on weekends.
We decided to stay home.
Do you mind waiting a few minutes?
He stopped smoking last year.

title: who / that / which / where
meaning: who / that / which: describes the noun before it
why: who for people, which for things, that for both, where for places. When it's the object, you can drop it: the movie (that) I saw.
form: the man who / that lives next door
the car which / that I bought
the café where we met
us: Americans prefer “that” to “which” in defining clauses: “the book that I read”. Dropping “that” in speech is very common.
examples: That's the guy who fixed my car.
Is this the book you were talking about?
I found a place where we can park.
The phone that I bought broke after a week.

quiz.q: This is the restaurant ___ we had dinner.

options: The shirt that I bought it is blue.
The shirt I bought is blue.
The shirt who I bought is blue.

title: Passive: is made / was built
meaning: something was done (what matters is the thing, not who did it)
why: When what happened matters more than who did it: The car was stolen. be + V3; to say who did it, add by…
form: is / are + V3 · was / were + V3 · has been + V3
English is spoken here.
us: In American speech, “get” often replaces “be”: “He got fired” “We got paid” “I got stuck in traffic”.
examples: My bike was stolen last night.
He got fired for being late.
The building was built in the sixties.
Dinner is served at eight.

quiz.q: I ___ stuck in traffic for an hour.
quiz.why: A “get” passive in the past → got

title: Reported speech: said / told
meaning: passing on what someone said
why: To pass on what someone said: said (that)… or told + a person + (that)… The tense usually moves one step back (is → was).
form: He said (that) he was tired.
She told me (that) she'd call.
He asked me if / where…
us: In American speech, if it's still true, people don't move the tense back: “She said she's coming.” Also “He was like…” instead of “said”.
mistakes: A reported question uses normal word order.
examples: She said she was running late.
He told me he'd call back.
They asked if we needed help.
My boss told us to finish by Friday.

quiz.q: He ___ that he liked the movie.

options: She asked me where was the station.
She asked me where the station was.
She asked me where is the station.

title: Phrasal verbs
meaning: a verb with a small word, usually with a new meaning
why: A verb + a small word (up, out, on, off…), and the meaning often changes: give up = quit. Some can be split (turn it off) and some can't (look after him).
form: turn on / off · pick up · find out · give up · look for · get along with
A pronoun goes in the middle: turn it off (not turn off it)
us: Everyday American speech is full of phrasal verbs: hang out, figure out, show up, run into. They matter more than formal words like “discover”.
mistakes: The pronoun goes in the middle.
examples: Can you pick me up at six?
I need to figure out what went wrong.
We hung out at the mall all afternoon.
Don't give up, you're almost there.

quiz.q: It's cold. Please turn ___ the heater.
I ran ___ an old friend at the store.

quiz.why: The pronoun goes in the middle

title: Question tags and “right?”
meaning: “right?” at the end of a sentence
why: At the end of a sentence to check: if the sentence is positive, the tag is negative (It's cold, isn't it?); if it's negative, the tag is positive (You don't smoke, do you?).
form: You're coming, aren't you?
She doesn't know, does she?
He went, didn't he?
us: Americans often say “right?” instead of the full tag: “You're coming, right?” “…, huh?” is casual.
mistakes: The tag uses the same helping verb.
examples: It's really hot today, isn't it?
You're coming tonight, right?
You don't eat meat, do you?
We met last year, didn't we?

quiz.q: The simplest tag in American speech:

title: too / enough / so / such
meaning: too much / enough
why: too = more than you want (too hot). enough = as much as you need (old enough / enough money). so + adjective, and such + a + adjective + noun, for strong feelings and results.
form: too + adjective · adjective + enough · enough + noun
so good · such a good movie
us: In speech, “so” is used a lot for strong feelings: “It's so good!” and “That's such a cool idea!”
examples: This coffee is too hot to drink.
Are you old enough to drive?
We don't have enough time.
It was such a long day.

quiz.q: The box is ___ heavy to carry.

title: Everyone is… / The team is…
meaning: words that mean a group but take a singular verb
why: everyone, everybody, nobody, and each are singular in English, even though they mean a group: Everyone is here. American English also treats groups (team, family, company) as singular.
form: Everyone / Nobody / Each + is / has
US: The team is… · My family is…
us: A clear American difference: “The team is winning” (British English may say “The team are…”). After “everyone”, people use “their”: “Everyone has their phone.”
examples: Everyone is waiting for you.
My family lives in Monterrey.
Nobody knows the answer.
The team is playing really well this year.

quiz.q: In American English: My company ___ hiring.
quiz.why: A group is singular in American English

title: gonna / wanna / gotta (American speech)
meaning: the short forms you hear in all American speech
why: In speech, Americans blend words: going to → gonna, want to → wanna, got to → gotta, kind of → kinda, let me → lemme, don't know → dunno. You need to understand them by ear. You can say them in everyday speech, but don't write them in a formal message.
form: gonna = going to (future) · wanna = want to · gotta = have got to
kinda = kind of · lemme = let me · gimme = give me · dunno = don't know
us: “gonna” is only for the future: “I'm gonna go”. Not for a place: “I'm going to Mexico City” can't be “gonna”.
examples: I'm going to grab some food.
Do you want to get some food?
I have got to finish this tonight.
Let me see your phone.

title: Third conditional: if + had done, would have done
pattern: If + had + past participle, … would have + past participle
meaning: if something had happened in the past, something else would have happened (but it didn't)
why: For a past that didn't happen (regret or imagination): if + had + V3, and would have + V3 in the result. If I had known, I would have come.
form: If + had + V3, … would have + V3
would have → would've (sounds like “woulda”)
us: In American speech you often hear “If I would have known…”, but it's wrong in writing; the correct form is “If I had known”. “would've” sounds like “woulda”.
mistakes: A past that didn't happen → had + V3.
“would of” is a spelling mistake for “would've”.
examples: If I had known, I would have called you.
We would have missed the flight if we hadn't left early.
If you had told me, I could have helped.
She wouldn't have said that if she'd been there.

quiz.q: If I ___ harder, I would have passed.
quiz.why: A past that didn't happen → had studied

quiz.q: If you had asked, I ___ you.

title: must be / might be / can't be
meaning: almost certain / possible / impossible (guessing)
why: To guess: must be = almost certain (from the evidence), might / may / could be = possible, can't be = impossible. For the past: must have been, might have been, can't have been.
form: must / might / can't + be / verb
The past: must have + V3 · might have + V3
us: In American speech, “might” is more common than “may” for “possible”. “You must be tired” is an everyday way to show you understand.
examples: You must be exhausted after that trip.
She might be stuck in traffic.
That can't be right.
He must have forgotten about the meeting.

quiz.q: The lights are off. They ___ be home.
I'm not sure. It ___ rain later.
She's not answering. She ___ have left already.
quiz.why: Almost certain, in the past → must have

title: I wish… / If only…
pattern: I wish + past / had + past participle
meaning: I want things (now or in the past) to be different
why: wish + past = you want the present to be different (I wish I had more time). wish + had + V3 = regret about the past (I wish I had studied). wish + would = you want someone to change what they do (I wish you would stop).
form: I wish + past (now) · I wish + had + V3 (the past)
I wish you would + verb (something that annoys me)
us: “I wish I was…” is common in American speech; the formal form is “I wish I were…”.
mistakes: Regret about the past → had + V3.
examples: I wish I had more free time.
I wish I hadn't said that.
I wish you would stop interrupting me.
If only we lived closer to the beach.

quiz.q: I wish I ___ to the party last night.
I wish it ___ raining. I want to go out.
quiz.why: You want someone to change → would

title: Present perfect continuous: have been doing
meaning: I've been doing something for a period of time
why: For something that started in the past and is still going on now (or just stopped, and you can see the result). The focus is on how long: I've been waiting for an hour.
form: have / has been + -ing
How long have you been…?
us: Everyday sentences: “I've been meaning to call you” = I've wanted to call you for a while. “What have you been up to?” = what have you been doing lately?
mistakes: From a time until now → have been.
examples: I've been working here for three years.
What have you been up to lately?
It's been raining since this morning.
I've been meaning to fix that door.

quiz.why: A length of time until now

quiz.q: Your eyes are red. ___ you been crying?
“What have you been up to?” means:
quiz.why: An everyday question about your news

title: have / get something done
meaning: I had someone else do something for me
why: When someone else does something for you (usually for money): I got my hair cut (at the barber). have / get + the thing + V3.
form: get / have + object + V3
I need to get my car fixed.
us: Americans use “get” more than “have”: “I got my phone repaired.” Also “get it done” = finish it.
mistakes: If someone else did it → got … cut.
The mechanic fixes it, not you.
examples: I got my hair cut yesterday.
We need to get the AC fixed.
She had her nails done for the wedding.
Where can I get this printed?

quiz.q: I'm going to get my car ___.
Which one is more common in American English?
options: I fixed my phone by someone.

title: I suggest he go (American subjunctive)
meaning: I suggest he do it: the base verb, even with he / she
why: In American English, after suggest, recommend, insist, and it's important that…, the verb is in its base form for every subject, even he / she: I suggest he call her.
form: suggest / recommend / insist + (that) + subject + base verb
It's important (that) she be on time.
us: This is very American; British English says “I suggest he should call”. In everyday speech Americans also say “I suggest calling her”.
examples: I suggest you talk to your manager.
The doctor recommended that she rest for a week.
It's important that he be there on time.
My parents insisted that I stay for dinner.

quiz.q: I recommend that he ___ a lawyer.
It's essential that everyone ___ the rules.

title: have / have got / gotten
pattern: Do you have…? · I've got… · It's gotten + adjective
meaning: I have, and “gotten” in American English
why: To say you own something: I have or I've got (same meaning). American English also has “gotten” as the third form of “get”: It's gotten better.
form: I have a car = I've got a car
Do you have…? (American) · Have you got…? (more British)
get – got – gotten (US)
us: The natural American question is “Do you have a pen?”, not “Have you a pen?”. The British don't use “gotten”, but Americans use it every day.
examples: Do you have a minute?
I've got a lot of work to do.
Traffic has gotten worse this year.
She's gotten really good at chess.

quiz.q: Which one is natural in American English?

options: I'm going to get a headache.

title: although / even though / despite / however
meaning: although + a sentence, despite + a noun
why: although and even though + a full sentence. despite and in spite of + a noun or -ing. however between two sentences (after a period or ;), meaning “but”.
form: Although it rained, we went out.
Despite the rain, we went out.
It rained. However, we went out.
us: In American speech, “but” and “though” at the end of a sentence are more common: “It was expensive. Worth it, though.” “however” is more for writing.
mistakes: “despite” isn't followed by a full sentence.
examples: Although I was tired, I finished the work.
Despite the traffic, we got there on time.
The hotel was small. It was really clean, though.
Even though he's rich, he lives simply.

options: Although it was cold, but we swam.
Although it was cold, we swam.
Despite it was cold, we swam.

title: What I need is… / It was… that…
pattern: What I need is… · It was … who / that…
meaning: focus: what I need is… / it was … who…
why: To put focus on one part of a sentence: What I need is a break. It was Alex who called (Alex, not anyone else).
form: What + subject + verb + is / was…
It is / was + the important part + who / that…
us: “What I mean is…”, “The thing is…”, and “All I want is…” are everyday American phrases.
examples: What I really need is a vacation.
The thing is, I don't have enough money.
It was my sister who told me.
All I want is a good night's sleep.

quiz.q: ___ I don't understand is why he left.
It was the noise ___ woke me up.

options: explain the real point or problem
quiz.why: explain the real point or problem

title: Never have I… / Not only… but also
meaning: formal focus: the helping verb before the subject after a negative word
why: In formal English and speeches: if you start with a negative word (Never, Rarely, Not only), the helping verb comes before the subject, like a question: Never have I seen this.
form: Never / Rarely / Seldom + auxiliary + subject…
Not only … but (also)…
No sooner had … than…
us: It's rare and formal in everyday American speech; people say “I've never seen anything like it”. You hear it in speeches and the news.
mistakes: The helping verb comes before the subject.
examples: Never have I seen such a beautiful view.
Not only is he smart, but he's also really kind.
Rarely do we get weather this nice.
I've never seen anything like it.

quiz.q: Not only ___ late, but he also forgot the tickets.
In everyday American speech, what's more common?

title: I do like it! (emphatic do)
meaning: stress: I really do / I really did
why: To stress something, or to answer someone who doubts you: do / does / did before the base verb, said with stress: I do care!
form: do / does / did + base verb (stressed)
She does know. · I did call you!
us: Americans use it in arguments: “I did tell you!” and “You do look tired.” Also in polite commands: “Do sit down.” (less common).
examples: I do understand how you feel.
I did tell you about the meeting!
She does look a lot like her mom.
We do need to talk about this.

quiz.q: You think I forgot? I ___ remember!
He ___ call you yesterday, I saw him.

title: Dropping words in speech: Sounds good. / Want some?
meaning: fast speech: the start of the sentence is dropped
why: In American speech, people drop the subject and helping verb at the start when the meaning is clear: (That) sounds good. (Do you) want some? (Are you) coming? You need to understand it by ear, and you can use it with friends.
form: Sounds good. = That sounds good.
Want some? = Do you want some?
Got it. = I've got it. · Been there. = I've been there.
us: This makes you sound very American, but in formal writing and work emails, write the full sentence.
mistakes: Only drop words from the start.
Dropping words is for speech, not formal writing.
examples: That sounds good to me.
Do you want some coffee?
I've got it, thanks.
Are you coming with us?

quiz.why: Formal writing needs a full sentence
